name: Elena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blasthole drill at an open-pit lithium mine. We drill rows of holes about fifteen metres deep across each bench, so the blast crew can load them and break the rock. I'm lead driller on day shift, and our newest drill has an assisted mode, so I can set it to drill a row on its own while I watch the second rig on a tablet. My morning starts with the drill plan from the engineers, I check it against the ground, then it's hole after hole. I like when the pattern on the screen matches the pattern on the dirt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is in your life, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Jonah, he's a carpenter, he builds kitchens. I use AI every day, at work to double-check drill logs and at home for my little drone business, I do crop and fence surveys for farmers on weekends. What wears me out is the heat on the benches in January and people at work who think the tablet is witchcraft. I've got maybe four months of bills saved, the rest went into the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Ha. Okay. Some people at work would love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd keep using it and I wouldn't argue with anyone about it. Online I'd post a drone video and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Lithium's growing anyway, batteries need it, so the mine's expanding. The AI I use would still save me a couple of hours a week, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling, keep the drone business going on weekends, maybe get one more farmer client a month. I'd put a bit more into savings, I'd like six months. Maybe ask about running both drills in assisted mode full time, because that's a pay grade up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some people at work would love that. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our blast supervisor, Geoff. He prints everything I send him and writes on it in pencil. He'd be thrilled if AI went away. I'd miss teasing him about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being bored, maybe. I like learning the next thing. But I'd find something, I always do, the drone thing started because I was bored in winter.

S0.say: It's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd keep using it and not argue with anyone about it.
S0.think: I'd be fine, because lithium is growing anyway and the mine's expanding. The AI I use would still save me a couple of hours a week, which is enough for me.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and grows the weekend drone survey business by about one farmer a month. Builds savings towards six months and asks to run both drills in assisted mode full time for the higher pay grade.
S0.quote: He prints everything I send him and writes on it in pencil.
S0.fieldNote: Elena works at a growing lithium mine, so even the quiet future looks good for her. She already uses AI and assisted drilling every day and has a weekend drone survey business. Her only worry is boredom, which she solves by starting new projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I'm already seeing, just more of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is just the next step, learn it or get left behind. I'd say it kindly at work, because I know it's harder for some people. And I'd offer to show anyone the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm already running two drills. In this picture I'd be running four from a control room, and they'd pay me more. My bigger worry would be Jonah, kitchens are hands-on but the designs and quotes would get automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First three months, I'd ask to be on the first team for the remote drill room. I'd do the short automation course the drill company runs. On weekends I'd push the drone business, add mapping for small mines and quarries. And I'd help Jonah set up an AI tool for his quotes, he hates paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Geoff, your supervisor with the pencil?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fifty-nine, he'd probably retire. I'd want the company to give him a decent package, not just push him out. He taught me how to read rock, that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the company would keep as many drillers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If I'm running four drills, that's three drillers who aren't. Some would go to maintenance or to the new pit they're opening. Some wouldn't. I'm not going to pretend that's fine for everyone.

S1.say: This is just the next step: learn it or get left behind. I'd say it kindly at work and offer to show anyone the tablet.
S1.think: It's good for me, because I'm already running two drills and I'd be running four from a control room for more pay. My bigger worry would be Jonah's quotes and designs getting automated.
S1.do: Volunteers for the first remote drill team within three months and takes the drill company's short automation course. Adds mapping for small mines and quarries to the drone business, and sets up an AI quoting tool for Jonah.
S1.quote: If I'm running four drills, that's three drillers who aren't.
S1.fieldNote: Elena sees steady change as a promotion and moves first without hesitation. She's honest that her gain means fewer drilling jobs for others, and hopes older colleagues get decent packages. Her concern shifts to her partner's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different animal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs a plan, starting this month. Businesses and the government both need to step up, and I don't care whose idea it is as long as it works. At work I'd stay practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my advantage disappears. If an AI can do anything, it doesn't need me to watch four drills. My drone business goes too, the farmers will just buy their own self-flying drones. I'd have maybe a year of being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the control room job straight away and save almost everything for a year. I'd sell the second drone. And I'd look at buying a small share in an automated survey service with a guy I know in the next town, so I own a piece of the thing instead of competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My brain would be running all night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said own a piece of the thing. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the machines do the work, the money goes to whoever owns the machines. I can't buy a mine, but I could buy a share in a small business that runs robots. It's a gamble, but sitting still is also a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having two years, rather than none, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to make one smart move, maybe two. Save hard, buy into something. It's not enough to build a whole new life. I'd be grabbing, not planning.

S2.say: Everyone needs a plan, starting this month. Businesses and government both need to step up, and I don't care whose idea it is as long as it works.
S2.think: My advantage disappears, because an AI that can do anything doesn't need me watching four drills. My drone business goes too, so I'd have maybe a year of being useful.
S2.do: Takes the control room job at once and saves almost everything for a year. Sells the second drone and looks at buying a share in an automated survey service, so she owns part of the machines instead of competing with them.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her mind running all night.
S2.quote: It's a gamble, but sitting still is also a gamble.
S2.fieldNote: Even a fast adopter like Elena loses her edge here and says so plainly. Her answer is ownership: buying into the machines rather than fighting them. She admits two years means grabbing, not planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five. Okay. That's tight but workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we're practical about it. I'd tell people at work to get skills that still matter for a few years, like maintenance and electrical. Online I'd share how-to stuff, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I do well for three or four of those years. I'd be running the drills from the control room, maybe the whole drill fleet. By year five I want to own something, not just be paid by someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, take the control room job and push to six months' savings. Turn the drone thing into a proper registered business with one employee, probably my cousin, using AI for all the booking and reports. Start looking at a share in a robot survey company in year two or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy and focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about him doing the business side with me, or keeping his kitchens as long as people still want a handmade kitchen. Some people will pay extra for a person, at least for a while. That might be his thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to Japan to see my grandparents is the one thing I wouldn't cut. Everything else, sure. Takeaways, new phone, all that.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if we're practical. I'd tell people to get skills that still matter for a few years, like maintenance and electrical.
S3.think: I'd do well for three or four years, running the drills or even the whole drill fleet from the control room. By year five I want to own something, not just be paid by someone.
S3.do: Takes the control room job and pushes savings to six months in year one. Registers the drone business with one employee and uses AI for bookings and reports, then looks at buying into a robot survey company in year two or three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but mostly busy and focused.
S3.quote: By year five I want to own something, not just be paid by someone.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Elena shifts from grabbing to building a business she owns. She thinks some customers will pay extra for human work for a while, which she sees as her partner's niche. She'd protect a family trip to Japan while cutting other spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready if people start now. I'd be the one at work running little sessions on the new systems. I'd say it calmly, panic doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Ten years is enough to build a real business, pay off something, maybe own a small fleet of survey robots. The end point bothers me for other people more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stay on the drills and move up to the control room. I'd register the drone business and save for the first proper survey machine. Jonah and I would probably buy a small house in year two or three, now we've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a bit guilty about being calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know Geoff and half the drill crew won't feel calm. Ten years is a lot for me at twenty-seven. For them it's ten years of watching their trade go. I'd want to help where I can, show them things, but I can't fix it for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to own something instead of just reacting. With two years I'm grabbing at shares in someone else's business. With ten I could build my own, slowly, the way I like doing things.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to get ready if people start now. Panic doesn't help, so I'd run little sessions on the new systems at work.
S4.think: I'd do well, with time to build a real business, pay something off and maybe own a small fleet of survey robots. The end point bothers me more for other people than for me.
S4.do: Stays on the drills and moves into the control room in year one. Registers the drone business, saves for a first proper survey machine, and plans to buy a small house with Jonah in year two or three.
S4.feel: Calm, with a bit of guilt about being calm when others won't be.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lot for me at twenty-seven. For them it's ten years of watching their trade go.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Elena feels calm and plans to build her own robot survey business. Her guilt comes from seeing how differently older colleagues will feel. Her centre politics show in a focus on practical steps over blame.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only one where I can't get ahead of it, I'd just be grabbing. What would help is clear rules on small businesses owning robots, so it's not just the giant companies, and cheap loans for people like me to buy in early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd want to own. Everyone asks what job you'd do. Nobody asks what you'd want to own when the jobs go. That's the real question, I think.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks what you'd want to own when the jobs go.
portrait: Elena Nakamura is 27 and the lead blasthole driller on day shift at a growing open-pit lithium mine, already running two drills with assisted automation. She lives with her boyfriend Jonah, a kitchen carpenter, uses AI every day and runs a weekend drone survey business for farmers. She has about four months of savings, the rest having gone into her drone. Pragmatic and in the middle politically, she moves first in every scenario and sees steady change as a promotion. With two years she grabs for shares in automated businesses; with ten she plans to build her own robot survey business, while feeling guilty about older colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it's the only scenario where she can't get ahead of the change.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules that let small businesses own robots, not just giant companies, and cheap loans so people like her can buy in early.
